title: Law & Your Rights · Episode 2
chapters: Separation of powers: why no one holds all the keys
Contracts: the deals you make every day
The snail in the bottle: how negligence law was born

units.t: Law & Your Rights. Episode two.
In this episode: Separation of powers: why no one holds all the keys, Contracts: the deals you make every day, The snail in the bottle: how negligence law was born and Your rights as a consumer.
Part one. Separation of powers: why no one holds all the keys.
Who makes the laws, who carries them out, and who decides what they mean?
Keeping those three jobs apart is one of the oldest safeguards against tyranny, and Australia does it in its own distinctive way.
Three keys to one vault.
Imagine a vault that needs three keys turned at once, held by three different people.
No one can empty it alone.
That is the idea behind the separation of powers.
The legislature makes laws; in Australia, that is Parliament.
The executive runs the country day to day, including the Prime Minister, ministers and the public service.
The judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes: the courts.
If one group controlled all three, it could write any rule, enforce it however it liked and judge its own case.
The French thinker Montesquieu made the case in The Spirit of the Laws, 1748: liberty is at risk when one body both makes and enforces laws, or when judges are not separate from rulers.
His reading of England was imperfect, but his argument shaped modern democracies.
The American model.
The framers of the United States Constitution in 1787 took Montesquieu seriously.

They placed Congress, the President and the Supreme Court in separate articles and kept their members apart: the President does not sit in Congress, and members of Congress cannot serve in the cabinet.
They added checks and balances so each branch can restrain the others.
The President can veto bills, Congress can override a veto with a large enough majority, the Senate must approve many appointments, and the courts can strike down laws that breach the Constitution.
Supporters say this makes power hard to abuse.
Critics say it can make government slow and prone to deadlock when rival parties control different branches.
Australia's blend.
Australia's founders borrowed from two traditions.
From the United States came a written Constitution with separate chapters: Chapter I covers Parliament, Chapter II the executive and Chapter III the courts.
From Britain came the Westminster system of responsible government, where ministers must sit in Parliament and answer to it.
Section 64 says a minister must become a senator or member of the House within three months.
So Parliament and the executive overlap heavily: the government is formed by whoever holds the confidence of the House of Representatives.
What keeps this in check is that ministers can be questioned in Parliament every sitting day, can lose the House's confidence, and must face voters at regular elections.
Keeping judges apart.
Where Australia is strict is the judiciary.

In the landmark 1956 Boilermakers' Case, the High Court ruled that a federal body could not combine judicial power, such as deciding legal guilt and punishment, with non-judicial functions like setting wages through arbitration.
Judicial power under Chapter III must be exercised by courts, and courts should not be handed tasks that compromise their independence.
Later cases extended some protection to state courts too, because they can exercise federal power.
Judges are also protected in other ways.
Federal judges can be removed only by the Governor-General after both houses of Parliament ask, on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, and their pay cannot be cut while they hold office.
Checks in everyday politics.
Once you know what to look for, checks appear everywhere.
The Senate rejecting or amending a bill is one house checking another.
Senate estimates hearings, where officials are grilled on spending, are Parliament checking the executive.
A court ruling a government decision unlawful is the judiciary checking the executive.
Auditors-General, ombudsmen and anti-corruption commissions add more, and a free press and the right to vote act as checks from outside government.
There is no perfect division.
Separate power too strictly and government can grind to a halt.
Concentrate it and those in charge may escape accountability.
Britain relies heavily on convention, the United States has rigid separation, and Australia sits between.
People tend to value checks more when their side is out of power.
The key idea: Government power splits into three jobs, and keeping them apart makes abuse of power harder.
Part two. Contracts: the deals you make every day.
Your morning coffee, your phone plan and your job are all contracts.
Knowing how they work helps you avoid nasty surprises.
Agreements the law enforces.
A contract is an agreement that the law will enforce.
You make them constantly: buying a coffee, tapping onto public transport, signing up for a streaming service, accepting a job or leasing a flat.
In Australia, contract law comes mainly from judge-made common law, with legislation like the Australian Consumer Law layered on top to protect consumers.
Every contract starts with an offer: a clear promise to be bound on certain terms.

Goods on a shelf and most advertisements are usually only an 'invitation to treat', which is why a shop usually isn't obliged to sell a wrongly priced item, although misleading pricing can breach consumer law.
Acceptance must match the offer.
'I'll take it for $50 less' is a counter-offer, which rejects the original.
What makes it binding.
Courts generally look for offer, acceptance, consideration, intention to create legal relations, capacity and reasonably certain terms.
Consideration means each side gives or promises something: you pay, the café hands over coffee.
So a bare promise of a gift usually can't be enforced.
It needn't be fair: selling a car for one dollar can be valid, though a court may check for pressure or deception.
A deed can bind without consideration.
Business deals are presumed to be legally binding; family and social arrangements, like cooking dinner for a friend, are presumed not to be.
Under-18s can often escape contracts, with exceptions such as necessities, and rules vary by state.
Someone lacking mental capacity may also be able to avoid a contract.
Written or verbal.
A common myth is that a contract must be written and signed.
Most can be verbal, or formed through emails, texts or clicking 'I agree' online.
The problem with verbal contracts is proof: in a dispute, it's your word against theirs.
Some contracts must be in writing to be enforceable, notably contracts for the sale of land and certain consumer credit contracts.
For anything important, like building work, a loan to a friend or a business arrangement, put the key terms in writing.
Include the price, what's being delivered, deadlines and what happens if things go wrong.
When a deal is broken.
Failing to do what a contract requires is a breach.
The usual remedy is damages: money to put you in the position you'd have been in had the contract been performed, not to punish the other side.
For a serious breach, such as breaking an essential term, the innocent party may be able to end the contract.
Occasionally a court orders actual performance, called specific performance, mostly for unique things like land.
Contracts can also be set aside for misrepresentation, duress or unconscionable conduct.
Time limits apply to claims, commonly six years in many states.
Unfair terms and cooling-off.

In take-it-or-leave-it contracts, like phone plans, the Australian Consumer Law protects against unfair terms: those causing a significant imbalance that aren't reasonably necessary to protect the business, such as letting only one side change the price.
A court can void it, and since November 2023 relying on unfair terms is also illegal.
Many people believe every contract has a cooling-off period.
It doesn't: those rights exist only where a law or the contract creates them.
Unsolicited sales, such as door-to-door, carry 10 business days under the Australian Consumer Law.
Residential property buyers usually get a few days, such as five business days in NSW, but not at auction.
Never sign under pressure.
This is general information only; for big contracts, see a lawyer or Legal Aid.
The key idea: A contract is an agreement the law will enforce, and it needs a clear offer matched by acceptance.
Part three. The snail in the bottle: how negligence law was born.
A woman in a Scottish café sipped a ginger beer and claimed she found a rotting snail in it.
Her lawsuit changed the law for almost everyone in the English-speaking world.
A snail and no contract.
On 26 August 1928, May Donoghue drank ginger beer from a dark, opaque bottle at the Wellmeadow Café in Paisley, near Glasgow.
A friend had bought it.
When the rest was poured into her ice cream float, she later said, the decomposed remains of a snail slid into her glass.
She claimed shock and gastroenteritis.
The trouble was legal.
If a faulty product hurt you, your main route was usually to sue the seller for breach of contract.
She had no contract with the café owner, who had neither made the drink nor sealed the bottle.
She had none with the manufacturer, David Stevenson, either.
Earlier cases suggested that a manufacturer owed nothing to a stranger, except for inherently dangerous items.
Up to the Lords.
Mrs Donoghue had little money, so she was allowed to sue as a pauper, without paying the usual court costs.
Her lawyer, Walter Leechman, took on the manufacturer.
The case reached the House of Lords, then Britain's highest court, which ruled in May 1932.
The judges did not decide whether a snail had really been in the bottle.
They answered a preliminary question: assuming everything she said was true, did the law give her a claim?
By three votes to two, they said yes.
A manufacturer who sells a product meant to reach the consumer unchanged owes that consumer a duty to take reasonable care.
Who is my neighbour.
The most famous judgment came from Lord Atkin, who reached for the parable of the Good Samaritan, in which a lawyer asks, 'Who is my neighbour?'
Atkin gave a legal answer.
You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions that you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour.
And your neighbour is anyone so closely and directly affected by what you do that you ought to have them in mind.
This was a broad principle, not a narrow rule about ginger beer.
A duty of care can exist between strangers wherever harm is foreseeable and the relationship is close enough.
Lawyers call it the neighbour principle, and first-year law students still learn it.
What negligence requires.
Donoghue v Stevenson gave shape to negligence, the law of careless harm.
Broadly, a person suing must show three things.
First, the other side owed them a duty of care.
Second, the other side breached it by falling below the standard of a reasonable person in their position.
Third, the breach actually caused harm of a kind the law recognises.
These ideas now sit behind claims about car crashes, medical mistakes, slippery supermarket floors and unsafe buildings.
Courts have spent decades refining where duties begin and end, because a duty that stretched forever would make everyone liable for everything.
Many places, including Australian states, have also passed laws limiting some claims and damages.
The snail travels.
A Scottish decision about a Paisley café could have stayed local.
Instead, in the mid-1930s, an Australian case reached the Privy Council in London, then Australia's final court of appeal.
Dr Richard Grant had developed severe dermatitis from woollen underwear made by Australian Knitting Mills, which contained irritating chemicals left from manufacturing.
Relying on Donoghue v Stevenson, the Privy Council held the manufacturer liable.
Courts in Canada and New Zealand followed, and governments later built consumer protection laws on these foundations.
Here is the twist.
David Stevenson died before the trial on the facts, and the claim was settled out of court.
No judge ever ruled on whether the snail existed.
A memorial now marks the café site.
The key idea: A woman who said she found a snail in her ginger beer had no contract with anyone, so the old law seemed to leave her without a remedy.
Part four. Your rights as a consumer.
'No refunds' signs, 'take it up with the manufacturer', 'the warranty's expired'.
Australian consumer law says otherwise more often than you think.
One national law.
Since 1 January 2011, one national law, the Australian Consumer Law, has protected consumers across Australia.
It sits in a schedule to the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 and applies the same way in every state and territory.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, ACCC, enforces it, together with agencies such as NSW Fair Trading and Consumer Affairs Victoria.
It covers consumer guarantees, product safety, misleading conduct, unfair contract terms, unsolicited selling and more.
You are generally a consumer if you buy goods or services normally used for personal or household purposes, or anything costing up to $100,000.
Guarantees and remedies.
Consumer guarantees apply automatically, whatever the receipt or store policy says, and businesses can't exclude them.
Goods must be of acceptable quality, safe, durable, free from defects, for a reasonable time, fit for any purpose you told the seller about, and match their description.
Services need due care and skill and must be delivered in reasonable time.
A $2,000 fridge should last far longer than a $20 kettle.
For a major failure, such as an unsafe item or one you wouldn't have bought knowing the problem, you can choose a refund or replacement, or keep it and claim compensation.
For a minor failure, the business can choose to repair, replace or refund.
If it refuses or takes too long, you can get it fixed elsewhere and claim reasonable costs.
Refund myths.
You have no legal right to a refund just because you changed your mind; that's store policy.
But 'no refunds' signs are misleading if they suggest you have no rights when goods are faulty.
The retailer can't send you to the manufacturer.
Proof of purchase can be a bank statement or online order, not only the receipt.
Sale items are covered too, unless the defect was pointed out before you bought.
A manufacturer's warranty is a promise on top of your guarantees, not a replacement.
Guarantees can continue after the warranty ends if a product fails sooner than expected.
Before buying an extended warranty, ask what it offers beyond the law.
Misleading conduct and scams.
The law bans misleading or deceptive conduct in trade.
That includes false claims about quality or origin, fake 'was' prices that inflate a discount, and fine print that contradicts the headline offer.
Businesses must generally show a single total price including compulsory fees, not hide charges until the end, drip pricing.
Large supermarkets must show unit prices, such as price per 100 grams.
Exploiting someone who clearly doesn't understand a deal, unconscionable conduct, is also prohibited.
Scams include fake parcel texts, calls impersonating banks or police, investment schemes and romance scams.
Warning signs are pressure to act now, unusual payments like gift cards or crypto, and requests for personal details or remote access.
Call back on a number you find yourself.
If you've lost money, contact your bank, then report to Scamwatch.
IDCARE offers free support.
Making a complaint.
Start with the business.
Gather your proof of purchase, photos and messages, explain the problem, and say which remedy you want under the consumer guarantees.
Putting it in writing creates a record.
If that fails, contact your state or territory fair trading agency, which can give advice and may help negotiate.
Industry ombudsmen handle specific sectors for free, such as the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman, energy and water ombudsmen, and the Australian Financial Complaints Authority.
For money claims, state tribunals like NCAT or VCAT are cheaper than courts.
Legal Aid and community legal centres can also help.
This lesson is general information only.
The key idea: The Australian Consumer Law gives the same protections in every state and territory, enforced by the ACCC and state agencies.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why does splitting government into three branches protect against abuse?
Answer. No one group can make, enforce and judge the rules.
Question two. Why isn't a shop usually obliged to sell an item that was wrongly priced?
Answer. Shelf prices are usually just an invitation to treat.
Question three. Why did Mrs Donoghue seem to have no legal claim?
Answer. She had no contract with the seller or the maker of the drink.
Question four. Who enforces the Australian Consumer Law?
Answer. The ACCC and state fair trading agencies.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
